overview: Unilever is a global consumer goods company headquartered in London and Rotterdam, selling branded Beauty & Wellbeing, Personal Care, Home Care and Foods products (including Hellmann's, Dove, Knorr, Vaseline, Axe, Domestos, Lifebuoy and Surf) in around 190 countries. The company reports in euros despite its LSE primary listing. Following the demerger of its Ice Cream business (The Magnum Ice Cream Company, TMICC) completed in December 2025 and an 8-for-9 share consolidation, Unilever now operates as a four-Business-Group continuing entity with FY2025 turnover of EUR 50.5bn, and in March 2026 it announced a further major portfolio reshaping: combining most of its Foods business with McCormick & Company in a ~USD 44.8bn transaction expected to close by mid-2027.

business_model.summary: Unilever makes money selling fast-moving branded consumer products through a vast global distribution network to retailers, wholesalers and (increasingly) direct digital/e-commerce channels, who in turn sell to end consumers. Revenue is largely recurring/repeat-purchase (household staples bought frequently) rather than project-based, driven by a mix of volume growth, pricing/mix and innovation-led premiumisation. 78% of FY2025 turnover came from 'Power Brands.' The FY2025 demerger of Ice Cream (continuing operations now exclude it; Ice Cream generated EUR 7.7bn turnover before demerger, now reported in discontinued operations) and the March 2026 announced combination of most of the Foods business with McCormick (excluding India Foods) are reshaping the revenue mix toward Beauty, Wellbeing and Personal Care.

revenue_streams.name: Beauty & Wellbeing
revenue_streams.trend: growing (USG +4.3% FY2025); pending further M&A reshaping (Dr. Squatch, Minimalist, Wild)

revenue_streams.name: Foods
revenue_streams.trend: stable but subject to pending McCormick combination, closing mid-2027

business_model.customer_type: B2C via retail/wholesale/e-commerce channels (B2B2C); large professional/food-service channel through Unilever Food Solutions
business_model.geographic_mix: Emerging markets ~59% of FY2025 turnover (Asia Pacific, Latin America, Africa, India), developed markets ~41% (North America, Europe); US and India are designated anchor growth geographies

main_competitors: McCormick & Company (post-Foods combination, as a shareholder/partner rather than pure competitor)
competitive_position.market_position: One of the largest global consumer packaged goods companies, with leading or top-tier share positions in categories such as deodorants, skin cleansing, oral care and savoury food/bouillons; trades at a valuation discount to P&G and Colgate (roughly 13x TTM earnings vs ~22-24x peers per analyst commentary), reflecting weaker historical execution and TSR versus peers

moat_factors.description: Multi-decade, category-leading Power Brands (Dove, Vaseline, Knorr, Hellmann's, Axe, Domestos, Lifebuoy) with 78% of turnover; high consumer trust and shelf presence across ~190 countries
~59% of turnover from emerging markets, built over decades (e.g., Hindustan Unilever in India); deep rural/general-trade distribution networks are hard for new entrants to replicate
EUR 836m annual R&D spend and science-led premiumisation (e.g., Dove Bio-Protein Care, K18 HeatBounce) support premium pricing, though company itself concedes it lags leaders in brand execution
Ranked #2 overall (and #1 in Foods and Personal Care) in the Advantage Group retailer survey, supporting shelf space and joint business planning
3.7bn people use a Unilever product daily, giving unmatched reach for new product launches and bolt-on brand acquisitions

weaknesses: History of underperforming peers on total shareholder return (significantly underperformed peers in the five years to end-2023 per the Chair's own statement)

Complex, frequently-reshaped portfolio (Ice Cream demerger FY2025, pending Foods/McCormick combination) creates execution and continuity risk and complicates investor understanding of 'steady-state' Unilever
Currency translation volatility from euro reporting against a basket of emerging-market currencies materially swings reported (though not underlying) growth and EPS
Lower R&D/marketing intensity than best-in-class peers in certain categories (e.g., trails L'Oreal in premium beauty per analyst commentary)
Reliance on third-party retailers/distributors for shelf space, exposing Unilever to private-label competition and retailer bargaining power

growth_drivers: Volume-led growth algorithm: management targets mid-single-digit underlying sales growth with at least 2%-3% underlying volume growth, aiming for 'top third' total shareholder return versus peers

Portfolio premiumisation and shift toward Beauty, Wellbeing and Personal Care, including bolt-on M&A (Dr. Squatch, Minimalist, Wild, Nutrafol, Liquid I.V.) and divestiture of lower-growth/non-core brands (Conimex, The Vegetarian Butcher, REN, Kate Somerville)
Anchor growth geographies: United States (largest market, regained share in FY2025) and India (improving momentum, Hindustan Unilever premium M&A)
Digital commerce and premium channel expansion

Productivity and simplification programme: SKU reduction (>30% since early 2024 in Beauty & Wellbeing, >20% in Personal Care since 2022, >25% since 2019 in Foods), supply chain vertical integration and AI-enabled operations supporting gross margin expansion (46.9% in FY2025, up 20bps)
AI adoption across R&D (faster formulation/simulation), marketing content creation (Brand DNAi, Beauty AI Studio, Sketch Pro) and supply chain to reduce costs and speed time-to-market

Planned Foods/McCormick combination (if completed) and residual TMICC stake monetisation expected to simplify the portfolio further, sharpen capital allocation toward a 'pure-play' Home & Personal Care plus Beauty & Wellbeing company (~EUR 39bn revenue base on FY2025 figures), and fund continued capital returns (~EUR 6bn of buybacks targeted 2026-2029)

business.description: Rapidly evolving consumer behaviour, digital commerce growth and new retail formats could erode brand relevance and market share if Unilever fails to innovate and market effectively (principal risk, unchanged level per FY2025 10-K equivalent)

Company-flagged increasing risk: sub-optimal capital allocation across Business Groups/markets/channels, and complexity from concurrent major portfolio moves (Ice Cream demerger just completed; Foods/McCormick combination pending) could destroy value or distract management

Large simultaneous organisational transformation (new operating model, AI rollout, category-dedicated sales forces) could create disruption; company notes this risk level decreased post-Ice Cream demerger but remains material given the pending Foods separation

business.risk: Safe and high-quality products / product liability
business.description: Contamination, mislabeling or product defects across a vast global supply chain could trigger recalls and reputational damage
Reliance on large retail customers for shelf space and promotional support; private-label competition pressures margins in mature markets

financial.description: Euro-denominated reporting against revenue generated ~59% in emerging markets (Latin America, India, Turkey) caused a (5.9)% currency drag on FY2025 turnover and (8.8)% drag on underlying EPS growth

Net debt of EUR 23.1bn at FY2025 year-end (2.0x underlying EBITDA), rising to EUR 26.0bn (2.3x) at H1 2026 following buybacks and M&A; management targets ~2x net debt/EBITDA while sustaining 'strong single A' credit ratings and ~EUR 6bn of buybacks through 2029
Free cash flow fell to EUR 5.9bn in FY2025 (from EUR 6.3bn) partly due to higher taxes linked to the Ice Cream demerger; further separation costs expected for the Foods/McCormick deal

regulatory.description: The ~USD 44.8bn Foods combination with McCormick requires Hart-Scott-Rodino and other antitrust/foreign investment approvals and McCormick shareholder approval; a former FTC chair has flagged likely close scrutiny given consumer price impact, and the deal does not require a Unilever shareholder vote, which has fueled investor and governance criticism
Extended producer responsibility schemes, plastic bans and sustainability mandates raise compliance costs and require packaging reformulation at scale

Broad regulatory footprint (product/ingredient safety, antitrust, anti-bribery, sanctions, data privacy, human rights due diligence) across ~190 countries creates fine/litigation exposure; merged into a single principal risk category in FY2025
Carbon pricing, land-use restrictions and GHG-intensive ingredient regulation could raise costs and constrain operational flexibility over the medium-to-long term

macro.description: Company-flagged increasing risk: escalating armed conflicts, rising protectionism/tariffs, and political instability following global elections, compounded by >50% emerging-market revenue exposure to FX and price controls
Raw material and packaging cost fluctuations cannot always be passed through via pricing without hurting volumes; partly hedged through forward buying

macro.risk: Consumer spending slowdown in subdued markets
macro.description: Management explicitly guided FY2026 growth to the 'bottom end' of the 4-6% USG range initially (later raised mid-year) reflecting slower market conditions, particularly in Latin America

macro_factors.industry_outlook: Global FMCG/personal care and home care markets are growing at low-single-digit volumes with price/mix providing incremental growth; premiumisation (beauty, wellbeing, prestige personal care) is outgrowing staple categories; emerging markets remain the larger growth engine despite near-term currency and macro volatility
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate - staple household/personal care products are relatively defensive, though discretionary premium/prestige lines and out-of-home food service exposure carry some cyclicality
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate - net debt of ~EUR 23-26bn and ongoing large buyback/M&A programme mean financing costs and credit ratings matter for capital allocation flexibility, though cash generation is strong (~100% cash conversion target)
key_input_costs: Agricultural commodities (palm oil, vegetable oils, dairy inputs for the former Ice Cream/current Foods business)

recent_developments.event: Completed the demerger of the Ice Cream business as The Magnum Ice Cream Company (TMICC), listed in Amsterdam, London and New York; Unilever retained a 19.85% stake to be sold down over time
Completed 8-for-9 share consolidation intended to maintain comparability of per-share metrics before and after the Ice Cream demerger

Announced combination of most of Unilever's Foods business (excluding India) with McCormick & Company in a transaction valuing Unilever Foods at an enterprise value of ~USD 44.8bn; Unilever shareholders to hold 55.1% of the combined entity plus a 9.9% direct Unilever stake, expected to close by mid-2027
Unilever shares fell roughly 7% (about $7bn of market value) on the McCormick deal announcement amid investor concern over integration complexity and regulatory risk; McCormick shares also fell

Reports of growing investor/employee backlash against the McCormick deal, including Terry Smith (Fundsmith) reportedly selling his entire Unilever stake citing a shift away from traditional shareholder interests toward activist-driven dealmaking; Unilever's Board called the decision unanimous
Completed a EUR 1.5bn share buyback tranche (started 30 April 2026); company reaffirmed a target of ~EUR 6bn of buybacks over 2026-2029 funded partly by separation-related cash receipts

Raised full-year 2026 underlying sales growth guidance to within the 4-6% multi-year range (from 'bottom end') with ~3% underlying volume growth, after Q2 USG of 5.8% beat the ~4.3% consensus estimate; H1 2026 net debt rose to EUR 26.0bn (2.3x underlying EBITDA) from EUR 23.1bn (2.0x) at FY2025 year-end

Analyst ratings remain mixed post-McCormick announcement: UBS and Jefferies cut to Sell/Underperform in October 2025 (pre-deal) on execution concerns, while broader consensus (TipRanks/valueinvesting.io) still skews toward Buy/Moderate Buy with average price targets clustering around 5,000p, well above the ~4,600-4,700p trading range seen in early October 2026

guidance.as_of: H1/Q2 2026 results (July 2026), building on FY2025 Annual Report (Chair's/CEO's statements)

items.target: 4%-6% (multi-year range); FY2026 now expected within this range (raised from 'bottom end')
items.notes: At FY2025 results, management guided FY2026 USG to the bottom end of the 4-6% range reflecting slower market conditions; at H1/Q2 2026 results (July 2026) this was raised to 'within' the full range after Q2 USG of 5.8% beat consensus of ~4.3%, with H2 2026 USG guided to 4%-5% led by pricing
12 consecutive quarters of positive underlying volume growth as of FY2025; all four Business Groups delivered positive UVG in FY2025
FY2025 UOM was 20.0%, up 60bps; medium-term 'growth algorithm' targets modest margin improvement fuelled by gross margin expansion
FY2025 actual was 2.0x; H1 2026 actual rose to 2.3x (EUR 26.0bn net debt) reflecting buybacks and bolt-on M&A; management maintains ~2x target alongside 'strong single A' credit ratings
FY2025 underlying ROIC was 19.0%, slightly down from 19.1% in FY2024
FY2025 cash conversion was 100%; free cash flow was EUR 5.9bn, down from EUR 6.3bn due to demerger-related tax costs
FY2025 returned EUR 6.0bn to shareholders (EUR 4.5bn dividends, EUR 1.5bn buybacks); quarterly dividend of EUR 0.4664/share declared at H1 2026

Funded by operational cash flow plus proceeds from the TMICC stake sell-down and Foods/McCormick separation; a EUR 1.5bn tranche was completed 5 June 2026 and a further EUR 1.5bn buyback was announced for 2026 at FY2025 results

items.target: Bolt-on M&A only; 'no transformational M&A' via traditional acquisitions
items.vs_prior: maintained in spirit, though the McCormick Foods combination (announced March 2026) is itself a transformational portfolio move structured as a combination/separation rather than a conventional acquisition
items.notes: Capital allocation framework explicitly favors bolt-on M&A (Dr. Squatch, Minimalist, Wild) alongside portfolio reshaping (demergers/separations) over large conventional acquisitions

guidance.management_commentary: Chair Ian Meakins and CEO Fernando Fernandez (since March 2025) describe 2025 as a 'decent year' with 'much still to do,' citing successful execution of the Ice Cream demerger, volume-led growth (12 consecutive quarters of positive UVG) and gross margin expansion, while acknowledging historic underperformance versus peers on TSR (significantly behind peers for the five years to end-2023, though +26.8% vs peer average -8% over the two years to the FY2025 report). Management explicitly frames 2026 markets as 'likely to remain subdued' but raised guidance mid-year after a strong Q2. The Board has stated confidence in the Foods/McCormick transaction despite investor pushback (e.g., Fundsmith's Terry Smith exiting the stock) and reiterated that the deal positions continuing Unilever as a focused Home & Personal Care plus Beauty & Wellbeing company.

bull_case: Simplified, higher-growth portfolio: completed Ice Cream demerger and the pending McCormick Foods combination would leave a focused ~EUR 39bn Beauty, Wellbeing, Personal Care and Home Care business with structurally higher margins and a cleaner growth narrative

Demonstrated momentum: 12 consecutive quarters of positive underlying volume growth, FY2025 gross margin expansion to 46.9% and underlying operating margin to 20.0%, with H1 2026 USG beating consensus and guidance raised mid-year

Valuation discount to peers: trading around 13x trailing earnings versus ~22-24x for P&G and Colgate per analyst commentary, offering re-rating potential if execution continues to improve and TSR catches up to the top third of peers (company's explicit ambition)

Strong, growing capital returns: ~EUR 6bn of buybacks targeted 2026-2029 plus a ~60% dividend payout ratio, supported by ~100% cash conversion and funded in part by TMICC stake monetisation and Foods separation proceeds

Deep emerging-market distribution and brand equity (3.7bn daily users, ~59% of turnover from emerging markets) provide a long-duration growth runway as these markets develop, alongside anchor-market momentum in the US and India
bear_case: McCormick Foods combination carries material execution, integration and antitrust risk; the ~7% share price drop on announcement, lack of a Unilever shareholder vote, and high-profile investor defections (Fundsmith's Terry Smith) signal real governance and value-creation concerns, with closing not expected until mid-2027

Chronic TSR underperformance versus peers over the five years to 2023 raises doubt about management's ability to sustain the recent improvement, especially given CEO (March 2025) and CFO are both relatively new to their roles

Heavy and growing currency translation drag (euro reporting against emerging-market currencies) materially understates underlying performance in reported figures and creates earnings volatility largely outside management's control

Rising leverage (net debt/EBITDA up to 2.3x at H1 2026 from 2.0x at FY2025 year-end) amid simultaneous buybacks, bolt-on M&A and separation costs could constrain flexibility if macro conditions deteriorate further

Repeated, back-to-back major portfolio restructurings (Ice Cream demerger just completed, Foods/McCormick combination now pending) create ongoing distraction, stranded costs and execution risk, and make it harder for investors to underwrite a stable, comparable multi-year earnings base
